title: The backward pass gathers what forward reused

blocks.text: The input shape is part of the backward contract. An input with shape (3,) and one with shape (1,3) may broadcast to the same two-row output, but their gradients must return to different shapes. The first has an inserted leading axis; the second has an existing singleton axis. The numeric contributions can be identical while the shape requirements differ.
Reduce an upstream NumPy gradient to an input shape that was broadcast in the forward pass. Sum inserted axes and singleton dimensions.

Broadcasting lets one input entry participate in multiple output positions. Reverse-mode differentiation asks how a final loss changes with that one input. Contributions from every output position that reused it must therefore be added, not averaged.

The example receives upstream gradients [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]]. Original entry zero was used in two output positions, so it receives 1+4=5. Entry one receives 2+5=7, and entry two receives 3+6=9. Follow one column in the animation. The repeated forward uses become converging backward paths.

blocks.text: Connect the picture to the mathematics

blocks.caption: Y is the broadcast output, x is the original input, and L is a scalar objective. The sum gathers all forward uses of input entry k.

blocks.text: The supplied implementation first sums leading axes until the upstream gradient has the same number of axes as the original shape. It then sums axes whose original size was one, preserving those dimensions with keepdims=True. Finally it reshapes to the original shape. This ordering prevents axis indices from referring to the wrong positions after earlier reductions.

Averaging the contributions would be a different derivative. If a scalar is used in ten additions, all ten paths contribute to its gradient. Whether the overall objective later divides by a batch size is separate; that division is already reflected in the upstream gradient. Also note that this helper assumes the gradient comes from a valid forward broadcast. It is not a complete validator for arbitrary incompatible shapes. Test both inserted axes and existing singleton dimensions, including a scalar input.

notes.text: Inserted leading axes are removed by summation.
Existing singleton axes keep their positions while collecting repeated uses.

checks.prompt: An entry receives upstream contributions 2 and 5 through two broadcast uses. What input gradient should it receive?

explanation.correct: The chain rule adds both paths: 2+5=7.
explanation.default: Revisit the stated quantities and units. The chain rule adds both paths: 2+5=7.

checks.prompt: A scalar is broadcast to four entries with upstream gradients 1, 2, 3, and 4. What scalar gradient returns?

explanation.correct: All four output positions reused the same scalar, so their gradients sum to 10.
explanation.default: Revisit the stated quantities and units. All four output positions reused the same scalar, so their gradients sum to 10.
